title: Privacy by Design
learning_outcomes: Explain the main security concern and trust boundary involved in Privacy by Design.
Choose an appropriate defensive control for Privacy by Design and state the assumptions under which it works.
Define a safe, reproducible verification step for Privacy by Design, including a relevant negative or failure case.

content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 24: Privacy and Data Protection. It builds practical understanding of Privacy by Design with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: Privacy by Design turns a security intention into evidence, an operational owner, and a repeatable control. Collect only data needed for a documented purpose, restrict access, avoid sensitive values in URLs/logs, set retention/deletion rules, and verify the complete data lifecycle.

content_blocks.title: Visual model: Privacy by Design
content_blocks.alt_text: Four-stage visual model for Privacy by Design: Define purpose; Minimize collection; Control access + retention; Verify deletion.
content_blocks.caption: Concept map for Privacy by Design. It is a learning aid, not a substitute for the stated control conditions.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Privacy by Design can be understood through this sequence: Define purpose → Minimize collection → Control access + retention → Verify deletion. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 179.1 Default privacy settings; 179.2 Limiting access to sensitive data; 179.3 Pseudonymization and anonymization concepts; 179.4 Privacy-friendly telemetry; 179.5 Evaluating data protection trade-offs. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Collect only data needed for a documented purpose, restrict access, avoid sensitive values in URLs/logs, set retention/deletion rules, and verify the complete data lifecycle.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.title: Safe reference example: Privacy by Design
content_blocks.expected_output: A data inventory records a purpose, access boundary, retention window, and deletion/anonymization action.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use synthetic data. Actual retention periods and legal obligations must be set by the responsible organization for its jurisdiction and purpose.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a clean local test account and synthetic data. Reset the test fixture after recording the result; do not include credentials or private data in the course report.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Collect only data needed for a documented purpose, restrict access, avoid sensitive values in URLs/logs, set retention/deletion rules, and verify the complete data lifecycle. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “Privacy by Design”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for Privacy by Design in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.
recap: Privacy by Design is a security boundary/control topic, not a standalone checklist item.
Collect only data needed for a documented purpose, restrict access, avoid sensitive values in URLs/logs, set retention/deletion rules, and verify the complete data lifecycle.
Retest fixes and record sanitized evidence; use only authorized environments.
